newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr bounces as RBA repeats wage concerns.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr bounces as RBA repeats wage concerns.

text.p: The Australian dollar rallied against its U.S. counterpart on choppy afternoon trade after the Reserve Bank reiterrated its concerns about wages growth, so dampening speculation it may yet ease policy again.
RBA governor Ian Macfarlane said recent wages figures had been a setback to prospects for low inflation, repeating the position he took in testimony to Parliament last week.

The emphasis quashed early rumours the bank was pondering another cut in official interest rates and helped the dollar rise to US$0.7775/80 by 2.00 pm (0400 GMT) from US$0.7733/38 just ahead of the speech and US$0.7745/50 at the opening.

In a speech on monetary policy, economic growth and unemployment, Macfarlane said it need more than high growth to reduce unemployment and Australia had a long way to go on supply-side reforms before the bank could be confident they had significantly lifted the country's potential growth rate.
Analysts saw this as a broadside to those commentators here who wanted the RBA to cut rates by as much as it took to get growth strong enough to reduce unemployment.
Indeed, much of the speech was a critique of the Australian labour market which concluded that over-regulation was chiefly resonsible for keeping unemployment so high.
Macfarlane noted the government had taken some steps to free up the labour market but his best guess was that this had not completed the process.
The best contribution monetary policy could make to bring down unemployment was to keep inflation under control so that the expansion could continue as long as possible, he said.

Thus most analysts concluded that since recent wages data implied a threat to inflation the RBA would not risk another cut. The latest figures on average weekly ordinary time earnings for full-time employees showed stronger than expected growth of 1.3 percent in the three months to February.
That took annual wages growth to 4.6 percent from 3.9 percent the quarter before and into the 4.5-5.0 percent zone which the RBA has expressed concerns about in the past.

Some, however, felt the wages danger was exaggerated and the breakdown of private and public sector AWOTE, to be released on May 22, would support their argument by showing growth had been biased upwards by special circumstances in the public sector.

They figure that if private sector growth -- which is far more indicative of demand and supply pressures in the economy -- was indeed well below the aggregate level, then the RBA could still have scope for a rate cut.

Traders said this argument clearly had some adherents in the market since the June 90-day bank bill contract was actually five basis points higher after the speech at 94.05, implying a rate of 5.95 percent against the present official 6.00 percent.

The dollar had a wild time on the crosses as US$/yen went into a tailspin overnight. Panic Japanese selling drove the U.S. currency down as far as 115.60 yen at one point before steadying on comments from the Ministry of Finance that the G7's desire for a lower dollar had fully filtered through to the market.
The AUD settled at 90.39/49 yen from a 89.70 low, but was still far below Wednesday's 92.57/67. -- Wayne Cole 9373 1800
